summary: Defines a Proxy Mobile IPv6 mobility option for negotiating GRE encapsulation and exchanging GRE keys, used to mark upstream and downstream traffic for a mobility session. It can also negotiate GRE without keys. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Each trip between two helpers gets a numbered tag on its packages, so they can tell which package belongs to which person.

questions: what is the gre key option
subtitle: A Proxy Mobile IPv6 option that lets a gateway and an anchor agree on GRE tunnels and per-session keys.

tldr.problem: Plain IPv4 or IPv6 tunnels between a mobile access gateway and a local mobility anchor cannot always tell which mobility session a packet belongs to, for example when different operators reuse the same private IPv4 address space.
tldr.mechanism: A new GRE Key mobility option, carried in the Proxy Binding Update and Acknowledgement, negotiates GRE encapsulation and swaps a downlink key and an uplink key that mark each session's packets. The option can also request GRE with no keys.
tldr.outcome: Both ends can now identify a session by the GRE key in each tunneled packet. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and is not marked as obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 5845 is a Proposed Standard from June 2010, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of the GRE Key option for Proxy Mobile IPv6.

sections.title: Why Plain Tunnels Are Not Enough
sections.content:
In Proxy Mobile IPv6 (RFC 5213), a mobile access gateway (MAG) and a local mobility anchor (LMA) carry a mobile node's traffic through a tunnel. RFC 5213 and RFC 5844 allow IPv6 and IPv4 encapsulation for that tunnel, as specified in RFC 2473 and RFC 2003.

The RFC points out scenarios where those modes cannot uniquely identify the destination of packets for a specific mobility session. It needs an encapsulation with richer semantics, and finds it in Generic Routing Encapsulation (RFC 2784) with the Key extension from RFC 2890.

The document defines a GRE Key option for negotiating the GRE encapsulation mode and exchanging the uplink and downlink GRE keys. It also lets the two ends agree on GRE without exchanging keys. It has no impact on IPv4 or IPv6 mobile nodes.
sections.eli5: When many people share one pipe, it is hard to tell whose package is whose. A number on each package fixes that.

sections.title: Keys, Directions and Policy
sections.content:
The RFC names two traffic directions inside the MAG-LMA tunnel. Downlink traffic is tunneled at the LMA and heads toward the MAG. Uplink traffic is tunneled at the MAG and heads toward the LMA.

Each direction has its own key. The downlink GRE key is assigned by the MAG and used by the LMA to mark downlink packets of a session. The uplink GRE key is assigned by the LMA and used by the MAG to mark uplink packets.

Whether GRE alone, or GRE with keys, is needed is decided by a policy check. The RFC says this policy could be per MAG-LMA pair, per LMA, per mobile node, or a combination.

The keys apply to the individual mobility binding updated by the Proxy Binding Update, not to all bindings a mobile may have registered under RFC 5648.
sections.eli5: Each direction of the trip gets its own tag. One side writes the tag for packages going one way, and the other side writes the tag for the packages coming back.

sections.title: Negotiating GRE and Exchanging Keys
sections.content:
For GRE mode only, the MAG includes the GRE Key option in its Proxy Binding Update but omits the GRE Key Identifier field. If the LMA supports GRE and processes the update successfully, it answers with a successful Proxy Binding Acknowledgement carrying the option, again without the identifier. No keys are used.

For GRE with keys, the MAG puts the downlink key in the GRE Key Identifier field of its initial Proxy Binding Update. If the LMA accepts after its policy check, it returns the uplink key in the same field of a successful acknowledgement.

Once a session has keys, the LMA MUST keep the same uplink key for the life of the session, although it MAY change it for administrative reasons such as a reboot, and some packet loss may result. On a Binding Lifetime Extension the MAG MUST send its downlink key again, and the LMA MUST return the same uplink key.

On an inter-MAG handoff, the new MAG may pick a new downlink key or reuse the previous MAG's key. Transferring that context between MAGs is out of scope.
sections.eli5: One helper writes a number and sends it over. The other helper answers with a number of its own. From then on, each uses the agreed number on packages going the right way.

sections.title: What the MAG and LMA Must Do
sections.content:
Each side stores the new information with its existing records. The MAG extends its Binding Update List entry, and the LMA extends its Binding Cache entry, with four fields: a GRE-encapsulation-enabled flag, the downlink key, the uplink key, and a flag for the UDP-based TLV-header format. That last flag is TRUE only when UDP tunneling and GRE are both enabled for the session.

The status codes steer the exchange:

  • If the MAG sent no GRE Key option but the LMA's policy requires GRE, the LMA MUST reject the update with GRE_KEY_OPTION_REQUIRED, and the MAG SHOULD resend with the option.
  • If the MAG sent the option but the LMA decides GRE is not needed, the LMA SHOULD send a successful acknowledgement with GRE_KEY_OPTION_NOT_REQUIRED and no option. The MAG then falls back to RFC 5213 handling and MUST NOT include the option again for that session.
  • If the LMA accepts the update but returns no GRE Key option and not that status code, the MAG treats the LMA as not supporting the option and SHOULD NOT include it in later updates.

When a GRE packet arrives, the receiver MUST use the key as an additional identifier to pick the mobility session, then remove the GRE header. On de-registration the LMA cleans up the binding and the keys with it.
sections.eli5: Both helpers keep a notebook with the tag numbers. If one of them says tags are not needed, or are needed after all, they follow simple rules to get back in step.

sections.title: The GRE Key Option and Message Changes
sections.content:
The new mobility option has type 33 and a 4n alignment requirement. It has a Type field, a Length field, a Reserved field, and a 32-bit GRE Key Identifier. Length counts the option's octets after the Type and Length fields: a value of 2 means the identifier is not carried, and a value of 6 means a downlink or uplink key is carried. Reserved bits MUST be zero when sent and ignored on receipt.

The RFC also adds a T flag (TLV-header format) to the Proxy Binding Update and Proxy Binding Acknowledgement. In the update it asks for the TLV header when tunneling IPv6 or IPv4 packets in IPv4. In the acknowledgement it says the LMA supports that.

Three Binding Acknowledgement status codes are defined, shown below.
sections.eli5: The tag is a small card with a label and a number on it. There is also a little switch that says whether to use an extra wrapper.

sections.title: Carrying Data Packets
sections.content:
With GRE negotiated, the MAG and LMA encapsulate payload packets following RFC 5213 and RFC 5844, ensuring the GRE header is present. When UDP-based tunneling is used together with GRE, the TLV-header UDP format MUST be used. The header order is IPv4, UDP, TLV, GRE, then the payload.

The TLV header has a Type that is always 0, so the receiver can tell it apart from an IP version field. It also has a Next Header (for example 41 for IPv6 or 47 for GRE) and a 16-bit Length. A receiver that finds the length from the UDP header differs from the TLV length MUST discard the packet.

If the MAG sets the T flag and the LMA does not support the TLV format, the LMA replies with GRE_TUNNELING_BUT_TLV_HEADER_NOT_SUPPORTED. The MAG then MUST use GRE without UDP encapsulation, or it may retry with other options or de-register. The LMA MUST NOT set the T flag unless the MAG did.
sections.eli5: Sometimes the package goes inside an extra envelope. A short note at the front of the envelope says what kind of thing is inside and how big it is, and if the note and the envelope disagree, the package is thrown away.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Sending the GRE Key option in a Proxy Binding Update or Acknowledgement reveals the group a mobile node belongs to, as identified by its Network Access Identifier or IP address. That may help an attacker target the flows of a specific group.

The RFC says this can be prevented with confidentiality protection on those signaling messages, or on all tunneled data packets between the MAG and the LMA to hide the markings. With GRE, IPsec can be used in tunnel or transport mode to protect the GRE header, but the traffic selectors contain the GRE protocol number, and there is currently no mechanism to use the GRE key as a traffic selector.
sections.eli5: A visible tag number can tell a snoop which group a package belongs to. Locking the envelopes hides the tag.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Octets after Type and Length: 2 means no key, 6 means a key is carried.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Zero on send, ignored on receipt.

fields.name: GRE Key Identifier
fields.desc: The downlink or uplink GRE key; present only when keys are exchanged.

items.label: GRE_KEY_OPTION_NOT_REQUIRED
items.desc: Update accepted, but GRE and keys are not needed for this session.

items.label: GRE_TUNNELING_BUT_TLV_HEADER_NOT_SUPPORTED
items.desc: GRE negotiated, but the TLV-header format is not supported.

items.label: GRE_KEY_OPTION_REQUIRED
items.desc: Update rejected because GRE and keys are required.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Always zero; tells the TLV header apart from an IP header.

fields.name: Res.
fields.desc: Reserved; zero on send, ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Next Header
fields.desc: Protocol number of the payload header that follows, for example 41 for IPv6 or 47 for GRE.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Octets of payload after this header, excluding the TLV header itself.
